content: When multiple micronutrient powders (MNPs) or small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS) were included three days per week, they significantly reduced the iron gap, providing 96% and 84% of the Nutrient Reference Value (NRV) for iron, respectively. However, when SQ-LNS was included seven days per week, a gap remained for the non-target nutrient vitamin B12, achieving only 94% of the NRV. All fortified items substantially reduced the gaps for the non-target nutrient vitamin D. For further details, refer to Annex 10. At 6.9 months of age, vitamin A, folic acid, niacin, and magnesium were not associated with tolerable upper intake levels (ULs) because the ULs for these nutrients apply only to synthetic forms or pharmacologic agents. For all other target and non-target nutrients, no ULs were established for infants and young children (IYC). Model solutions exceeded ULs only for copper and zinc. For additional details, see Annex 9. In sensitivity analyses assuming lower iron absorption, the UL for zinc was exceeded in approximately half of the scenarios that included fortified items, while the UL for copper was exceeded in nearly all such scenarios. Refer to Annex 10 for further information. Macronutrient intakes, expressed as a percentage of energy, were relatively consistent across all feasible and liberalized best-case food patterns. Low-energy food patterns had a higher percentage of energy from protein, particularly for the oldest age group. Liberalized food patterns tended to have slightly higher protein percentages and lower carbohydrate percentages. For more details, see Annex 9. At 9 months of age, macronutrient distributions for all food patterns were within recommended ranges, although no specific ranges are set for infants. The macronutrient ranges for protein, fat, and carbohydrates varied across low, middle, and high energy levels. For example, protein ranged from 10-16%, fat from 35-40%, and carbohydrates from 45-60%. These estimates are based on Atwater factors to convert grams to kilocalories and then to percentages of energy. However, due to limitations in the food composition database, which reports total carbohydrates rather than available carbohydrates, these estimates are imprecise and may sum to more than 100%. They should be interpreted cautiously unless the excess or deficit is substantial. The percentage of energy from broad food groups, such as starchy staples, fruits, vegetables, dairy, and protein foods, varied across energy levels. For example, starchy staples contributed a higher proportion of energy at higher energy levels, while fruits contributed more energy at lower energy levels. Vegetables showed a consistent percentage of energy across energy levels, as the number of servings selected was generally the maximum allowed by model constraints. Dairy contributed a low percentage of energy, increasing slightly with energy levels but remaining below 6%. Protein foods contributed a higher percentage of energy at lower energy levels, particularly for non-breastfed children. Added fats and oils were not included in the food patterns for breastfed infants and young children (IYC). For non-breastfed children, the percentage of energy from added fats and oils decreased from 16% to zero in sensitivity analyses. This reflects that in the original analyses, iron needs were met, and protein was minimized. In sensitivity analyses where iron needs were not met, more protein foods were selected. Food group diversity was assessed across all age and feeding groups. Several food groups and subgroups were selected at their maximum possible amounts. For example, starchy staples were consistently included, while fruits and vegetables varied depending on the energy level and feeding group. Protein foods included both animal-source and plant-source subgroups, such as meat, fish, eggs, legumes, soy foods, nuts, and seeds. Dairy was included in some scenarios but not others. Minimum dietary diversity, defined as consuming foods and beverages from at least five out of eight defined food groups during the previous day, was achieved in most modeled food patterns. However, the modeled patterns are weekly, and the indicator is based on a single day. Food groups were counted even when weekly quantities were small. For further details on food group and subgroup selections, refer to Annex 9 and related tables.
